Task 1 · Tell us the story of each picture

the four pictures.

Each picture on its own, with its own story.

Picture 01

Marcus

The lake

Marcus had been sleeping in his car for eleven days when he drove to the lake.

The company had four months of runway left, which was generous depending on how you counted. His co-founder had left in March. The lead investor had gone quiet in June. He had stopped checking his email between midnight and six because nothing good came in during those hours and the bad things could wait.

He rented a boat and pushed out from the dock. He brought his laptop because he always brought his laptop. He sat in the middle of the lake and started writing down every assumption underlying the business, one by one, to see which ones he could actually defend.

He wrote for four hours. The lamp ran out of oil at some point. He kept going on the battery light. At some point he noticed a paper boat in the water near him, a kid’s thing, slowly filling and going under. He watched it sink. Then he closed the document, opened a new one, and started over from the beginning with only what he was sure of.

He had six assumptions left by the time the battery died.

Six was enough.

Story 01 of 04↗
Picture 02

Raya

The table in the wheat

Raya had been cooking for forty years.

He had set the table in the field because his mother had done it once, for a birthday, when Raya was seven. He remembered the long table in the wheat, the way the light came in sideways at that hour, the feeling that the world had been arranged specifically for this meal. He had been trying to recreate it ever since.

His wife was supposed to be there. His three children. His brother from Palermo had promised twice and cancelled twice before, so Raya had known about him, really. The neighbors he had been meaning to have over for three years. The old professor who had taught him to make pasta in 1987 and who was eighty-one now and still ate well.

One by one they had canceled.

He went anyway. He had the food. He had the table. He sat at the far end and ate slowly and watched the light change over the wheat. The glasses stayed full. The chairs stayed empty. He did not cry, which surprised him. He felt something closer to clarity, the recognition that he had been feeding people his whole life not because they asked but because he needed to, that the cooking was always the point and the people were the excuse.

He ate everything he could and left the rest on the plates.

Driving home, he called his brother, and they talked for an hour, which was longer than they had talked in years.

Story 02 of 04↗
Picture 03

David

The rope in the square

The rope had been there since the festival, which ended three weeks ago.

Nobody had come to collect it. It ran across the wet stone from somewhere near the fountain to somewhere near the church steps, thick and frayed at the ends. David had been eating his lunch on the church steps every day and looking at it.

On Friday he picked up his end.

He stood there holding it, not pulling, just holding. On the other side of the square, thirty or forty people were milling around the market stalls. He was not sure what he expected. He was not sure he expected anything.

Then a woman with a shopping bag grabbed the other end, almost as an afterthought, and leaned back.

More people joined her. They grabbed on one after another, laughing at first, then quietly, then seriously, the way people get when they realize they are actually doing something. David dug his heel into a crack between the stones and pulled back. The rope went taut. The pigeons went up.

He held his ground for a long time.

He was smiling. He did not know why exactly. Forty people on the other end, strangers, and he was holding his own, and it was raining a little now, and the lampposts had come on, and none of it made any particular sense.

He held on anyway.

Story 03 of 04↗
Picture 04

Thomas

The empty pool

The pool had been empty since October. Someone had spray-painted a small fish on the deep end wall, which made no sense and which Thomas had grown fond of.

He came every morning anyway. Coach Miriam came too, which he had not asked her to do. She just showed up the second week with her clipboard and her stopwatch and stood at the far end of the empty pool, and neither of them mentioned it.

He climbed to the board and went through his routine. Arms back. Chin level. Weight forward over the toes. The city spread out behind him, going pink and orange. Down below, Miriam clicked the stopwatch even though there was nothing to time. He had watched her do this for six years, and he still did not fully understand it. She said once that the stopwatch was not for the swimmer. He had not pushed her on what she meant.

He stood there longer than usual that morning. A cold wind came through, and the leaves that had collected in the deep end shifted around. Miriam wrote something on her clipboard. He could not see what.

He stepped off the board. The landing was harder than water, obviously, and he bent his knees to take it. He walked the length of the empty pool to where she was standing and looked at the clipboard.

She had written it before he jumped. He could tell by the ink how it had dried. One word at the top of an otherwise empty page, in her handwriting, which was small and certain.

Yes.

He stood there reading it for a moment. She took the clipboard back and tucked it under her arm and started walking toward the exit without saying anything.

He followed her.

They had coffee at the place on the corner that opened early. She ordered for both of them without asking, which she always did. They sat by the window and watched the street come to life and talked about the next six months and then about other things, and the coffee went cold, and they ordered more.

Task 3 · The documentary

one scene.

A short documentary about the first two years. This is my scene.

b · The title

The first Aperturians

a scene from year one

a · The scene

In the first three months, nobody called back.

Izuu sent the case files to sixty-three companies. He tracked every one of them in a spreadsheet: the date sent, the person, the company, whether they opened it. Most of them opened it. None of them replied.

He rewrote the first case file four times. He changed the structure, the length, the way the stories were sequenced. He tested different subject lines. He sent some with a personal note at the top and some without. He kept the spreadsheet updated and stared at it and could not find the variable that mattered.

Harsh asked him in week ten how it was going. Izuu told him the truth: nothing yet, but he had a theory about why, and he wanted two more weeks to test it.

Harsh said okay.

The theory was that the case files were landing in inboxes of people who recognised the problem but did not have the authority to do anything about it. He needed to be one level higher. He spent the next two weeks rewriting everything for a different reader, the CHRO, not the recruiter, and rebuilding the list from scratch.

The first reply came on a Thursday. A fintech company in Chicago. The head of HR said a colleague had forwarded her something and she had recognised her own company in it, a situation from four months ago she had told almost nobody about.

She asked how he knew.

He explained what he had been reading, what patterns had come up, how he had written them down.

She signed a contract the following week.

That night Izuu updated the spreadsheet. He added a new column he had not needed before: closed.
